content:
`.success()`, `.error()` and `.complete()` were deprecated in jQuery 1.8 and **removed in 3.0**. jqXHR is a Promise-compatible object, so the replacements are the Deferred method names:

| removed | replacement |
|---|---|
| `.success(fn)` | `.done(fn)` |
| `.error(fn)` | `.fail(fn)` |
| `.complete(fn)` | `.always(fn)` |

`.done` and `.fail` get exactly the same arguments in the same order as the callbacks they replace:

```javascript
$.ajax({ url: '/save', method: 'POST', data: payload })
  .done(function (data, textStatus, jqXHR) { /* ... */ })
  .fail(function (jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) { /* ... */ });
```

So for those two a straight rename is safe, including handlers that read the third argument.

`.complete` to `.always` is **not** a straight rename, and this is the one that will bite you. `.complete(fn)` always received `(jqXHR, textStatus)`. `.always(fn)` receives whichever set the settled state produced: `(data, textStatus, jqXHR)` on success, `(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown)` on failure. Any `.complete` handler that treated the first argument as a jqXHR now gets the response body on the happy path, silently.

If the handler only does cleanup (hide a spinner, re-enable a button) the rename is fine. If it reads arguments, keep a reference instead:

```javascript
const req = $.ajax(opts);
req.done(onData).fail(onError);
req.always(function () { setBusy(false); });           // argument-free cleanup
// or, when you really need the jqXHR:
req.always(function () { console.log(req.status); });  // req *is* the jqXHR
```

For the forty call sites: `.success(` to `.done(` and `.error(` to `.fail(` are mechanical, with one caveat -- `.error()` is also a jQuery *element* method on DOM objects in old code, so check that `$.ajax` appears in the same statement before you let a regex loose. Do the handful of `.complete(` by hand.

There is a parsing rule, and it is the one place where the *shape* of the string silently changes the timezone assumption.

The ECMAScript Date Time String Format defines two cases:

- **date-only** forms -- `YYYY`, `YYYY-MM`, `YYYY-MM-DD` -- are interpreted as **UTC**;
- **date-time** forms with no offset -- `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm` and longer -- are interpreted as **local time**.

`<input type="date">` gives you `'2026-03-01'`, the date-only form, so `new Date(input.value)` is midnight UTC. In Eastern Standard Time that instant is 19:00 on 28 February, and `getDate()` -- a local-time getter -- reports `28`. At UTC+1 the same instant is 01:00 on 1 March, everything looks right, and the bug waits a week. Appending `T00:00:00` moves the string into the second case, so it parses as local midnight and every local getter agrees with what the user picked.

Knowing that, the shift is not the thing worth patching -- the `Date` is. A calendar date has no instant attached to it, and `Date` cannot represent one. Every conversion afterwards is another chance to reintroduce this: a UTC server, a DST boundary, a `toISOString()` on the way to the API.

Cheapest correct fix is not to construct a `Date` at all:

```javascript
input.addEventListener('change', () => {
  save({ due: input.value }); // '2026-03-01' - keep the string
});
```

`YYYY-MM-DD` sorts correctly as a string and goes straight into a Postgres `date` or MySQL `DATE` column.

If you genuinely need the parts in JS, build the date instead of parsing one:

```javascript
const [y, m, d] = input.value.split('-').map(Number);
const local = new Date(y, m - 1, d);   // local midnight, no parsing rules involved
local.getDate();                        // 1
```

The multi-argument `Date` constructor is always local time with no format ambiguity, which makes it the better tool whenever you already have the numbers.

One trap on the way back out: if anything downstream does `d.toISOString().slice(0, 10)` on that local midnight, you get the same off-by-one in the other direction for users west of UTC. Rebuild the string from `getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate()`, or format with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`.

Keys are how React matches elements between two renders. With `key={i}` the keys are *positions*, not rows. After deleting B the list goes from keys `0,1,2` (A,B,C) to keys `0,1` (A,C). React sees key `1` in both renders and concludes it is the same element, so it keeps the DOM node that used to be B's and only updates the props that changed. `defaultValue` is what makes that visible. React writes it to the DOM node **on mount only** -- it is the uncontrolled initial value, and on updates React deliberately leaves the node's live `value` alone, because the user owns it. The node is not new, so nothing writes to it, and it still holds `B`. Your state array really is `[A, C]`, exactly as you observed. The uncontrolled file input has the same story: the `FileList` lives on the DOM node, and the node was reused. Switching to `value` + `onChange` did not fix the reuse. It made React overwrite the wrong node's value on every render, which hides the symptom and leaves the cause. Everything else attached to that node is still wrong: focus, scroll position, a running CSS transition, an open `
`, the file selection. Key by the row's identity: ```javascript {rows.map((row) => (
    • ))} ``` Now deleting B removes key `b`, key `c` is untouched, and React unmounts exactly one `
  • `. The index is a safe key only when the list is append-only and never reordered, filtered or sorted -- in practice, when nothing can shift an item's position for the life of the list. You already have `row.id` (the delete handler uses it), so you were never in that category. If you ever have rows with no stable id, generate one when the row is created (`crypto.randomUUID()`), never during render. A key produced in render is new on every render, which unmounts and remounts the entire list -- the same bug, worse.

The boundary is not protecting you from a crash. It marks the place where the prerender is allowed to stop. During `next build` there is no request, so there is no URL and no search params, and `useSearchParams()` in a client component cannot produce a value. React's answer is to render the nearest Suspense fallback into the static HTML and finish that subtree on the client once a real URL exists. With no boundary above the component there is nowhere to stop, so the only remaining options are "make the whole route dynamic" or "fail the build" -- Next picks the second and names the page. `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` takes the first option, for the entire route, which is exactly the static content you wanted to keep. Put the boundary around the smallest server-rendered parent of the chips: ```typescript import { Suspense } from 'react'; import { FilterChips } from './filter-chips'; export default function SearchPage() { return (

Search

}>
); } ``` Everything outside the boundary is prerendered as before; only the chips are deferred to the client. Three details decide whether this actually works: - the `` has to be **outside** the component that calls the hook. Putting it inside `FilterChips` changes nothing, because the component still has to render in order to reach it. - the fallback is real HTML that users see before hydration. Give it the chips' height, or you have traded a build error for a layout shift. - the boundary scopes one thing: which subtree is client-rendered on first paint. So it should cover everything whose *output* depends on the URL. If a heading also prints the active query, it belongs inside -- otherwise it gets prerendered with the wrong text and then hydrates to something else.

Before refactoring anything, check your exact Node minor. Node 22.12 unflagged `require(esm)`, so on a current Node 22 your original `require('chalk')` works as written. Hitting ERR_REQUIRE_ESM on "Node 22" means you are somewhere in 22.0-22.11.

```bash
node -v
```

If the build image can move to 22.12+ (or 24), the fix is a base image bump plus one small edit, because `require()` of an ES module returns the **namespace object**:

```javascript
const chalk = require('chalk').default;
```

Where that stops working, so you know what you are buying:

- if anything in the imported module graph uses **top-level `await`**, `require` throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` and you are back to `await import()`. That is a property of the dependency and it can appear in a patch release, which makes this the less durable of the two fixes.
- it only helps this repo. Anything you publish still has to work on whatever Node your consumers run.

There is a third option, and for a build script it is the one I would actually take: delete the dependency. `util.styleText` has been in Node since 20.12 and does what a build script wants from chalk:

```javascript
const { styleText } = require('node:util');

console.log(styleText('green', 'ok'));
console.log(styleText(['bold', 'red'], 'failed'));
```

It honours `NO_COLOR` and TTY detection, it is synchronous, it is CommonJS-native, and it removes the package that started this. For a script that prints three colours that is a smaller diff than either migration -- and one fewer dependency that can go ESM-only next quarter.

Second option, and the one I would take if this type is load-bearing: make the schema the source of truth at runtime and derive from that, rather than deriving a type from a type.

With a `const` object you are already most of the way there:

```typescript
const config = {
  api: { baseUrl: 'https://x', timeoutMs: 5000 },
  ui: { theme: { accent: 'red' } },
} as const;

type ConfigPath = Path<typeof config>;
```

That does not reduce the type-level work by itself, but the object literal is now the single source of truth, and the same paths can be produced by a five-line runtime walk -- which has no instantiation limit at all.

The step that actually ends the problem is codegen. Walk the object (or a zod/valibot schema's `shape`) in a small script and emit a plain literal union:

```typescript
// generated - config-paths.d.ts, do not edit
export type ConfigPath =
  | 'api'
  | 'api.baseUrl'
  | 'api.timeoutMs'
  | 'ui'
  | 'ui.theme'
  | 'ui.theme.accent';
```

A literal union of a few hundred strings costs the compiler essentially nothing, resolves instantly in the editor (recursive conditional types are also why autocomplete on `Path<T>` feels slow), and cannot produce ts(2589) however the config grows. The price is an `npm run gen:config` step and a generated file in the repo.

Be honest about the halfway house: `z.infer` is itself a recursive conditional type, so switching to a schema library moves the cost rather than removing it. What it buys you is runtime validation and a `shape` that is trivial to walk for the codegen above.

And before writing any of this: `react-hook-form` ships `FieldPath<T>`, which solves exactly this problem and has been tuned against large types for years. If it is already in the project, import it instead of re-deriving it.

Start with the two literals, because neither is the number you wrote:

```javascript
(1.005).toPrecision(20);   // '1.0049999999999998934'
(1.015).toPrecision(20);   // '1.0149999999999999023'
```

Both are stored slightly *below* the decimal you typed. `toFixed` rounds the stored value, correctly, so `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `'1.00'`.

Which also means one line of your question does not reproduce: in V8 `(1.015).toFixed(2)` is `'1.01'`, not `'1.02'`. Worth re-checking where the `1.02` came from, because `toFixed` is consistent here -- it rounds down in both cases, for the same reason. `Math.round(1.005 * 100)` is the same story from the other end: `1.005 * 100` is `100.49999999999999`, and `Math.round` of that is `100`.

`(0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2) === '0.30'` is not a counterexample either; the error there is far below the second decimal, so it rounds the way you expect. That is the real hazard with float money -- it is right almost always, and wrong on the invoice accounting looks at.

Yes: move to integer cents at the boundary. Do it in the layer that talks to the API, so nothing downstream ever holds a fractional amount:

```javascript
// one place, at the edge
const toCents = (n) => Math.round(n * 100);

const line = { qty: 3, unitCents: toCents(row.unitPrice) };
const totalCents = line.qty * line.unitCents;          // exact integer arithmetic
const display = (totalCents / 100).toFixed(2);         // only for rendering
```

`Math.round(n * 100)` is safe as the *entry* conversion even though it failed above: an API value with two decimals is at most half a cent away from its integer-cent value, and the float error is around 1e-14, so the rounding decision is never close. It is only the second rounding -- of an already-rounded amount -- that lands exactly on a tie and exposes the representation.

Integers are exact up to 2^53, so sums, multiplications by quantity and percentages-as-integers all stay exact, and the only rounding left in the system is the one you write on purpose when you divide (tax, splits) -- where you can pick the mode the finance team wants and test it.

If the amounts can exceed 2^53 cents, or you need decimal semantics all the way through, `BigInt` cents or `decimal.js` is the next step. For invoices, integer cents is nearly always enough.

Direct answer to the Intl half of the question, because it is more useful than it looks: **yes**, `Intl.NumberFormat` gives you the behaviour finance expects, and it does so for a reason worth understanding.

```javascript
const nf = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', {
  minimumFractionDigits: 2,
  maximumFractionDigits: 2,
});

nf.format(1.005);   // '1.01'
nf.format(1.015);   // '1.02'
nf.format(2.675);   // '2.68'
nf.format(8.575);   // '8.58'
```

Compare with `toFixed`, which returns `'1.00'`, `'1.01'`, `'2.67'` and `'8.57'` for the same inputs. The difference is not the rounding mode, it is what each one rounds. `toFixed` rounds the exact binary value (`1.0049999999999998934...`). `Intl.NumberFormat` rounds the *shortest decimal string that round-trips to that double* -- i.e. `"1.005"` -- so a tie stays a tie and half-expand does what a human expects. Since Intl NumberFormat v3 you can also state the mode explicitly:

```javascript
new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', {
  minimumFractionDigits: 2,
  maximumFractionDigits: 2,
  roundingMode: 'halfExpand',   // default; also 'halfEven', 'ceil', 'trunc', ...
});
```

`halfEven` is there if your accountants want banker's rounding, which is a decision worth asking about rather than assuming.

Two limits before you treat this as the fix:

- **It is a formatter.** It solves rendering. It does nothing for `a + b`, for summing 400 lines, or for a total computed in JS -- those still accumulate float error, and a total that is off by 1e-13 will occasionally cross a tie and format one cent away from the sum of its displayed lines.
- The same v3 also lets `format()` take a **string**, which is parsed as a decimal with no double in the middle: `nf.format('1.005')` is `'1.01'` exactly, not by luck. If you can get the API to send amounts as strings (`"12.34"`), you can render them with full precision and never construct the float at all.

So: `Intl` for display, and either strings or integer cents for arithmetic. Using `Intl` to paper over float arithmetic just moves where the missing cent shows up.

One thing worth ruling out before you conclude the load was the problem: SvelteKit **reuses the component instance** when you navigate between two URLs that match the same route. `/questions/1` to `/questions/2` does not create a new `+page.svelte`; it updates the `data` prop of the existing one.

That means a correct load can be re-running while the page still shows question 1, if the component copied the value once:

```javascript
// +page.svelte - broken, and it looks fine
let { data } = $props();
let question = data.question;   // read once, at init
```

`question` is a plain variable assigned during setup. New `data` arrives, nothing reassigns it, and the page never changes -- exactly the symptom you described, and a hard refresh "fixes" it because a fresh mount runs the initialiser again.

```javascript
// correct
let { data } = $props();
let question = $derived(data.question);
```

(Svelte 4: `export let data;` plus `$: question = data.question;`.)

Two other things in this family, since they all present as "the page did not update":

- **`onMount` does not re-run.** If you initialise a chart, a map, or an editor there and feed it `data.question`, it is initialised once for the whole route. Either update it in an `$effect` that reads the derived value, or force a remount with `{#key data.question.id}...{/key}` around the subtree.
- **Scroll position and focus** are also part of the same reuse. SvelteKit restores scroll per navigation, but a manually focused element or an open accordion carries over.

So the honest debugging order for "navigating between two ids shows the old one" is: check whether the load re-ran at all (a `console.log` in the load, server-side, tells you in one navigation), and only then look at the tracking rule. If the log fires with the new id and the screen is unchanged, the load was never the bug -- and switching to `params.id` will have looked like the fix while the real cause waits for the next component that copies `data`.

Adding the part that turns this from a fix into a rule, because it is the same bug in flexbox and it will come back in a nested container.

The automatic minimum size applies to **flex items too**: `flex: 1` is `flex: 1 1 0%`, and the `0%` is the flex-*basis*, not a minimum width. `min-width` still defaults to `auto`, which still resolves to min-content. A flex item containing a `<pre>`, a long URL or a `<table>` refuses to shrink for exactly the reason your grid track did. Same cause, same class of confusion, different property name.

The rule I apply: **any flex or grid item that can contain content of unknown width gets `min-width: 0`.** In practice that is every layout column, card body, and list item that renders user or CMS content.

The other half, which the grid fix alone does not give you: the constraint propagates through *every* ancestor between the track and the overflowing element. Fixing the outermost track is enough when the chain is one level deep. With a sidebar > article > section > pre nesting, each intermediate box with `width: auto` contributes its own min-content, so one of them can reintroduce the floor:

```css
.content > * ,
.content :where(article, section, div) {
  min-width: 0;
}
```

In Tailwind that is `min-w-0` on the column, and it is the single most useful utility in the framework for this reason.

Two related cases worth knowing, because they present identically:

- **`<table>`.** A table has its own intrinsic sizing and ignores `min-width: 0` in the way you expect. Wrap it in a `div` with `overflow-x: auto` and give *that* div `min-width: 0`, then the table scrolls inside its wrapper.
- **long unbroken text.** `minmax(0, 1fr)` makes the *track* correct, but the text still paints outside its box, because nothing told it it may break mid-word. Add `overflow-wrap: anywhere` for prose. The `<pre>` does not need it -- it has a scrollbar -- but a URL in a paragraph does, and it is a different property fixing a different thing. People frequently apply one and report the other as still broken.

Date parsing is standardised for exactly one grammar, and your string is not in it.

The spec defines the **Date Time String Format**, a simplification of ISO 8601: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`, with a `T` separator and an optional offset. Implementations are *required* to parse that. For anything else, the spec says the result is implementation-defined -- an engine may fall back to whatever heuristics it likes, including returning `Invalid Date`.

`'2026-01-05 10:00:00'` uses a space instead of `T`, so it is outside the required grammar. V8 has a lenient fallback parser and accepts it. JavaScriptCore has historically been stricter and returns `NaN`. Neither is a bug; you found the boundary of what is guaranteed.

So the immediate unblocking fix on your side is one character:

```javascript
const d = new Date(raw.replace(' ', 'T'));
```

But read the second half of your own question, because you are right to be suspicious: `'2026-01-05T10:00:00'` has **no offset**, and the spec says a date-time with no offset is interpreted as **local time**. So after that fix, the same string is 10:00 in Warsaw for one user and 10:00 in Los Angeles for another -- nine hours apart, from identical bytes. It will parse everywhere and be wrong somewhere, which is a worse bug than `NaN` because nothing throws.

(For completeness, the rule is inconsistent by design: a **date-only** string, `'2026-01-05'`, is interpreted as **UTC**, while `'2026-01-05T10:00'` is local. Adding a time changes the timezone assumption.)

The fix that is actually correct is an offset in the string, and that belongs on the API side -- see the other answers for the Python change. If you need to ship something before the backend moves, and you know for certain the API means UTC:

```javascript
const d = new Date(raw.replace(' ', 'T') + 'Z');
```

Append `Z` deliberately, with a comment saying you are asserting a contract the API does not currently state. That way when the API starts emitting offsets, the person removing this line knows what it was for.

The fix belongs on the API, and the Python change is one method call.

`str(datetime)` calls `datetime.__str__`, which is `isoformat(sep=' ')` -- a space separator, deliberately, because it is meant to be human-readable. It is not an interchange format and it does not claim to be. `datetime.isoformat()` gives you `T`, and a timezone-aware datetime carries the offset with it:

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone

# what you have now
str(datetime.now())                      # '2026-01-05 10:00:00.123456'  - space, no offset

# what to send
datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()   # '2026-01-05T10:00:00.123456+00:00'
```

The important half is `timezone.utc`, not `isoformat()`. A **naive** datetime (`datetime.now()`, or one read from a column declared without a timezone) has no offset to serialise, so `isoformat()` gives `'2026-01-05T10:00:00'` -- valid JavaScript, parsed as *local time in the browser*, which is the silent version of your bug. Make the datetime aware at the source, not at the serialiser.

With Django REST Framework or Pydantic this is already the default output; if you are hand-rolling JSON, a default encoder is the place to put it once:

```python
import json

def default(o):
    if isinstance(o, datetime):
        if o.tzinfo is None:
            raise TypeError('naive datetime in API response')
        return o.isoformat()
    raise TypeError(type(o))

json.dumps(payload, default=default)
```

The `raise` on naive datetimes is worth keeping. It converts "wrong timestamp on someone's phone, three weeks later" into a failing test on the first response that contains one.

`+00:00` and `Z` are both accepted by the JavaScript spec, so either is fine; `Z` is shorter and `isoformat()` in Python 3.11+ will produce it via `.isoformat().replace('+00:00', 'Z')` if you prefer it. (Python's own `fromisoformat` accepts `Z` from 3.11 on, so the round trip stays clean.)

Once the API emits an offset, `new Date(raw)` is unambiguous in every engine, your Safari bug is gone, and so is the class of bug where two users see different times for the same event.

There is, and it is a set of three. CSS Values 4 added viewport units that distinguish the two viewport sizes iOS switches between:

- `lvh` -- **large** viewport height: the viewport with browser chrome retracted. This is what `100vh` equals on iOS Safari, which is exactly the behaviour you measured.
- `svh` -- **small** viewport height: the viewport with the chrome expanded. The smallest the visible area gets.
- `dvh` -- **dynamic**: tracks the current state, changing as the toolbar collapses and expands.

For a hero with a button pinned to the bottom edge that must be visible on load, you want `svh`:

```css
.hero {
  height: 100vh;    /* fallback for anything without the new units */
  height: 100svh;
}
```

The section then fits inside the small viewport, so the button is above the toolbar on first paint, and it stays visible once the toolbar retracts (with a bit of space below it, which is the price).

`100dvh` is the one people reach for first and it is usually the wrong choice here. It is genuinely dynamic: the value changes while the user scrolls and the toolbar animates, so the section resizes mid-scroll. That means layout and paint on every step of that animation, plus content that visibly shifts under the user's finger -- the modern version of the jank you already have with the JS approach.

The cascade fallback is all the browser support handling you need: a browser that does not understand `100svh` drops that declaration and keeps `100vh`, which is what it does today. Support landed in Safari 15.4, Chrome 108 and Firefox 101, so on iOS 18 you are well inside it, and the fallback only serves genuinely old clients.

If you need to branch on availability for something more involved, `@supports (height: 100svh) { ... }` works. For this one declaration the two-line cascade is simpler and does the same thing.

Two limits of `svh`/`dvh` worth knowing before you consider this closed, both of which show up on the same device.

**1. The on-screen keyboard is not part of it.** None of `vh`, `svh`, `lvh` or `dvh` shrink when the software keyboard opens -- by default the keyboard overlays the viewport rather than resizing it. If your hero (or any full-height layout) contains an input, focusing it puts the keyboard over the bottom of your section, including that pinned button. The unit swap does nothing for this.

The declarative control is the viewport meta's `interactive-widget` key:

```xml
<meta name="viewport"
      content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover, interactive-widget=resizes-content">
```

`resizes-content` makes the keyboard shrink the layout viewport, so viewport units and `position: fixed` elements account for it. Support is not universal, so where it matters, `window.visualViewport` is the API that reports the truth:

```javascript
visualViewport.addEventListener('resize', () => {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--vvh', `${visualViewport.height}px`);
});
```

That is the same shape as the workaround you called dated -- and it is still the right tool for this one case, because it is the only thing that reports the *visual* viewport. The difference is that it now handles one narrow problem instead of standing in for `100vh`.

**2. `100dvh` and scroll-linked animation do not mix.** If you were tempted to use `dvh` instead of `svh`, be aware that the toolbar collapse is driven by scrolling, so a `dvh`-sized element resizes *during* the scroll it is reacting to. Anything positioned relative to it -- a sticky header, a scroll-driven animation, an `IntersectionObserver` threshold -- gets a moving reference frame, and the results are hard to reason about and harder to test. `svh` for sizing plus `dvh` only where you genuinely want the element to track the chrome (a bottom sheet, a fixed toolbar of your own) keeps that contained.

Practical order: `min-height: 100svh` for the section, `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` for the pin, `visualViewport` only if there is an input involved. The JS is not dated, it just has a much smaller job now.

The framework has a component for exactly this: `next/script`.

```typescript
// app/layout.tsx
import Script from 'next/script';

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        {children}
        <Script
          id="support-chat"
          src="https://vendor.example/widget.js"
          strategy="afterInteractive"
        />
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

What it does that a raw `<script>` tag does not: Next keeps a module-level record of scripts it has loaded, keyed by `src` (and by `id` for inline scripts). Render the same `<Script>` again -- on a client navigation, in a second layout, twice on one page -- and it does not load again. That is the "exactly once" guarantee you asked about.

A raw `<script>` in JSX gets none of that. It is a DOM element in the RSC payload, and it is inserted whenever React renders that part of the tree. The two symptoms you describe are the two ways it gets inserted twice: the browser executes it from the streamed HTML *and* React re-inserts it during hydration (your "briefly two on hard refresh"), and it is re-inserted whenever the subtree containing it remounts on navigation.

`id` is not optional here, even for an external script -- it is what Next uses for deduplication in several code paths, and adding it costs nothing.

On strategy, briefly:

- `afterInteractive` (the default) loads after hydration. Right for a chat widget.
- `lazyOnload` waits until the browser is idle. Better for a widget nobody uses in the first ten seconds, which is most support chat.
- `beforeInteractive` blocks hydration and is only valid in the root layout. A chat widget does not qualify; reserve it for consent managers and polyfills that must run first.

And the layout is the right place, provided the widget genuinely belongs on every route -- see the other answers, because "every route" is worth questioning and because `next/script` alone does not make the vendor's own snippet idempotent.

One diagnostic point, because "two launchers" has a second cause that none of the loading fixes address: the script may be running once and *rendering* twice.

Many widget snippets do something like this on load:

```javascript
var el = document.createElement('div');
el.id = 'vendor-launcher';
document.body.appendChild(el);
```

with no check for an existing node. So the duplicate can come from the vendor's own bootstrap running twice, from the widget being re-initialised by an `init()` call you make on navigation, or from a leftover DOM node that a previous instance appended and nothing removed.

Check which before choosing a fix:

```javascript
// how many script tags?
document.querySelectorAll('script[src*="vendor.example"]').length;
// how many launcher nodes?
document.querySelectorAll('[id^="vendor-"], iframe[src*="vendor.example"]').length;
```

The combination tells you where to look:

| scripts | launchers | cause |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | the script is loading twice -- `next/script` with an `id`, or a module-scope guard |
| 1 | 2 | one load, two initialisations -- you are calling `init()` on navigation, or the vendor re-bootstraps on `pushState` |
| 1 | 1, then 2 after nav | a node left behind by an unmounted component, plus a fresh one |

The middle row is the one people get wrong, because every fix they read about is aimed at the first. If it is yours, the answer is not in how you load the script -- it is to call `init` once and use `update`/`show` afterwards.

The last row is worth stating explicitly: **removing a `<script>` element does not undo its effects.** If you added the script from a `useEffect` and clean up by removing the node, the vendor's div, globals, listeners and websocket all survive; the next mount adds a second set. That is why the effect version reintroduced the duplicate in dev under StrictMode -- it was not really the double-invoke, it was that the cleanup did not clean anything up.

Whichever row you land on, add the idempotency guard anyway. Third-party snippets get re-run for reasons you do not control (a tag manager, a preview toolbar, a fast refresh), and a guard costs one line.

The option nobody mentions: for phone numbers specifically, hand-rolled formatting is a bigger commitment than it looks, and there is a well-maintained way out.

Your current formatter assumes nine digits in 3-3-3 groups. That is one country's landline convention. The moment the form accepts an international number, the grouping depends on the country and often on the prefix within it, and the rules change often enough that they are published as a data file rather than a regex.

```bash
npm i libphonenumber-js
```

```javascript
import { AsYouType } from 'libphonenumber-js';

function onChange(e) {
  const formatted = new AsYouType('PL').input(e.target.value);
  setValue(formatted);
}
```

`AsYouType` is built for this: it formats progressively as the user types and handles per-country grouping, so you are not encoding one country's convention in a regex that a support ticket will eventually contradict. You still need the caret restore from the other answers on top of it -- the library formats, it does not manage selection -- but the digit-index approach works unchanged, because "digits before the caret" is format-independent.

Two smaller notes on your markup, both correct as written and worth keeping:

- `inputMode="tel"` on a `type="text"` input is right. Do **not** switch to `type="number"` (it strips leading zeros, allows `e`, and shows spinners) or `type="tel"` if you plan to call `setSelectionRange` -- selection APIs are only defined for text-like inputs, and calling them on a `number` input throws `InvalidStateError` in Chrome. `type="tel"` does support selection, so it is a safe upgrade if you want the phone keypad without relying on `inputMode`; `type="number"` is the one to avoid.
- add `autoComplete="tel"` so browser autofill works. It is one attribute and it removes a large share of manual typing, which is the real fix for a formatting bug.

If the field only ever accepts one national format and always will, ignore all of this and keep the nine-digit version -- the library is 100+ kB for the full metadata set, and there are lighter metadata subsets if you need only a few countries. It is a trade to make deliberately, not a default.

The two settings you are relying on do different jobs, and neither is "check the runtime":

- **`target`** controls syntax downlevelling. It rewrites `async`, optional chaining, class fields. It never touches built-ins, because you cannot rewrite a method that does not exist.
- **`lib`** is a set of **declaration files**. It is a promise you make to the compiler about what the environment provides. `lib: ["ES2024"]` does not check anything -- it asserts `Object.groupBy` exists, and the compiler believes you.

You told the compiler the runtime is ES2024 and shipped it to a runtime that is not. Nothing was wrong from tsc's point of view, and there is no flag that would have caught it, because the tsconfig *is* the specification of the runtime as far as TypeScript is concerned.

So the fix is to make that assertion true, and to make it come from one place. For Node 20:

```json
{
  "extends": "@tsconfig/node20/tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}
```

```bash
npm i -D @tsconfig/node20 @types/node@20
```

`@tsconfig/node20` sets `lib: ["ES2023"]` and `target: "ES2022"` -- the values that actually match Node 20 -- so `Object.groupBy` becomes a compile error at the line that uses it, which is where you wanted the warning. `@types/node@20` does the same for the Node API surface, so you also stop using `node:` APIs added in 22.

Two things worth pinning down while you are in there:

- **`lib` should describe the runtime, `target` may be lower.** There is no benefit to `target: "ESNext"` on a server you control; matching both to the runtime keeps output readable and errors honest.
- **The `lib` value has to be maintained.** When you move to Node 22, you bump `@tsconfig/node22` and `@types/node`, and the new built-ins light up. That is the whole maintenance burden, and it is one line -- provided the tsconfig, the Dockerfile and CI cannot disagree about which version that is. See the other answers, because that disagreement is the actual root cause here.

The type layer is a symptom. The defect is that four things disagree about which Node this project runs on: your laptop (22), the tsconfig (implicitly 22 via `lib: ES2024`), CI (whatever its image defaults to), and the container (20). Fix the disagreement and the class of bug disappears, including the ones no compiler can catch -- a `node:` API added in 21, a change in `fs` behaviour, a native dependency's prebuilt binary.

Declare the version once and make everything read it:

```
# .nvmrc
20.18.1
```

```json
{
  "engines": { "node": ">=20.18 <21" }
}
```

```bash
# .npmrc - refuse to install with the wrong Node instead of warning
engine-strict=true
```

```
# Dockerfile - same version, pinned, not a floating tag
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine
```

```
# CI
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
```

Now `nvm use` on your laptop, the CI runner and the image are all on the same number, and that number lives in one file. `engine-strict` turns a mismatched local install into an immediate error rather than a difference you find in production three weeks later.

Two additions that pay for themselves here:

- **Build in the same image you run in.** If `npm run build` happens in CI on Node 22 and the artifact runs on Node 20, anything version-sensitive in the build (a bundler's target detection, a native module) is compiled against the wrong version. A multi-stage Dockerfile with the same `FROM` for both stages removes the question.
- **A smoke test on the built artifact.** One CI step that runs the built job with `--help` or against a fixture, inside the production image, catches `X is not a function` before deploy. It would have caught this one, and it catches the ones that are not about types at all.

The tsconfig change in the other answer is still worth making. But a correct `lib` on a project where the container version can drift independently is a fence with a gate left open.

One misconception worth naming explicitly, because it is what made this feel like it should have been caught: **no TypeScript setting emits a polyfill.** Not `target`, not `lib`, not `downlevelIteration`.

`tsc` transforms *syntax*. Set `target: "ES2015"` and it rewrites `async`/`await` into generators. It will not, ever, add an implementation of `Object.groupBy`, `Array.prototype.at`, or `String.prototype.replaceAll` -- those are library functions, and TypeScript's position is that supplying the runtime is your job. esbuild and swc behave the same way. This surprises people coming from Babel, where `@babel/preset-env` with `useBuiltIns` *does* inject core-js imports, which is the one toolchain in common use that blurs the line.

So if you want the API rather than a compile error, you have to ship the implementation:

```bash
npm i core-js
```

```javascript
// the entry point, before anything else
import 'core-js/actual/object/group-by';
import 'core-js/actual/map/group-by';
```

Import the individual features, not `core-js` wholesale -- the full package patches a very large surface and there is no reason for a job that needs one method to carry it. With that import at the top of the entry, `lib: ["ES2024"]` becomes an accurate description of the runtime *as you have configured it*, and the type layer and the runtime agree again.

Where I would and would not do this:

- **Worth it** when you need a spread of newer built-ins across a codebase, or when the runtime floor is genuinely out of your control (a published library, a browser bundle with a broad browserslist).
- **Not worth it here.** One method, one call site, on a server whose Node version you own. A polyfill is a dependency, a startup cost, and a global patch that other code can come to depend on invisibly -- so removing it later is harder than adding it was. The three-line helper or the Node bump are both smaller.

If you do add it, add the lint rule from the other answer too and put the polyfilled features on its allowlist. Otherwise the next person hits the same error with a different method and has no way to tell which built-ins this project has decided to guarantee.

Stepping back from the tooling: `node:20-alpine` in the Dockerfile while you develop on 22 is not a constraint to work around, it is the bug.

Node 20 left maintenance in April 2026. It is no longer receiving security patches, which makes "the container is on 20" a finding in its own right, separate from `Object.groupBy`. Every workaround in this thread -- narrowing `lib`, adding a lint rule, hand-rolling `groupBy`, importing a polyfill -- is work to keep an unsupported runtime viable.

```
FROM node:22.14.0-alpine
```

Then `lib: ["ES2024"]` is honest, the code you wrote works as written, and the disagreement between your laptop and production is gone rather than documented.

Two notes on doing it safely:

- **Pin the full version, not `node:22-alpine`.** A floating major tag means the base image moves under you between builds, which is a milder version of the problem you just had. Pin `22.14.0-alpine`, or the digest, and bump it deliberately. Same for `.nvmrc` and the CI setup step, so all three name one number.
- **20 to 22 is an LTS-to-LTS hop with a small blast radius**, but check native dependencies first (`npm rebuild` in a scratch container will tell you quickly), and check anything reading `process.version` or depending on V8 behaviour. Node 22 also brings `require(esm)` from 22.12, which can change how an ESM-only dependency behaves in a CommonJS file -- usually for the better, but it is a behaviour change worth knowing about before the deploy rather than after.

Keep the tsconfig and lint changes from the other answers regardless. They are what makes the *next* version gap visible: when Node 22 leaves support and someone has to move to 24, you want the compiler to tell you what changed rather than the deploy.

But the ordering matters. Configure the toolchain to describe the runtime accurately, then keep the runtime supported -- not the other way round, where you spend a year tuning `lib` values to stay compatible with an image nobody is patching.
